title: The Toll
part: PART FOUR: HOLDING UP THE BRIDGE

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: To err is human, to forgive is somebody else's job.*

Three days later, the sun came out. It was a bright that made the wet cobblestones shine like polished buttons. The old bridge was closed off with wooden planks and yellow tape. Safe as a sleeping dog. But the steps down to the arch were crowded.

The queue stretched all the way up the hill and around the corner of the Kettle & Crumb. People stood in the sun. They held their stories. A baker held a jar of honey and a confession about a sour temper. A schoolteacher held a poem she had never dared to read aloud. They went down one by one, into the cool shadow, and came back up looking lighter. As if they had handed over a heavy coat.

At the front of the line stood the Mayor. He was holding a small, folded piece of paper. It was very long, with many creases. He took it out. Smoothed it against his knee. Whispered the first word of his apology. It was a very long apology. It had several chapters. Hobb, who was sitting on a stool with his teacup, listened to every single one. Nodding his large, mossy head.
pages.image: A sunny street in a stone town with a long line of people waiting at wooden steps leading down into a dark archway; a man in a top hat stands at the front holding a paper, while a large grey-green troll sits inside drinking from a teacup.

pages.text:
Rue waited. She waited while the baker went. She waited while the teacher went. She waited until the last of the crowd had gone up the steps and the sun was getting low, painting the river in shades of gold and copper.

Then she went down.

Biscuit trotted at her heels, his orange tail high. In her pocket, her fingers were wrapped tight around the small, horn button. It was cold and smooth, and it felt like a secret that had been kept for too long. The arch was different now. The lantern was mended and glowing, and the moss garden had been replanted, growing in neat, curly patterns along the stone walls. Beside the old bucket, there was a second one, new and shiny.

Rue stopped. Her heart was beating very fast, a small bird trying to get out of her chest. She looked at Hobb. He was looking at her, his round spectacles mended with twine, his face soft and kind.
pages.image: A small freckled girl with curly red-brown hair in two puffs stands at the bottom of stone steps in a dark archway, an orange cat at her feet; a large grey-green troll with round spectacles sits nearby, and a glowing lantern hangs on the wall.

pages.text:
"I didn't come to be forgiven," Rue said, her voice trembling only slightly. "I came to tell you what my toll is."

Hobb waited, holding his teacup with both hands while the steam curled up between them like a shy cat.

"It's the whole story," Rue continued. "The lie, and how much I loved being your friend, and how sorry I am. And how I would give anything in the world to unring that bell." She swallowed hard. "It hurt me, Hobb. Not you. Me. It hurt me to hurt you."

Hobb looked down at his cup. The kettle in the corner hummed, a low, steady sound that filled the silence.

"It isn't ringing anymore," he said finally, his voice quiet. "It's a while ago now." He lifted his head, and his eyes were gentle. "I'll tell you something. When Willa said what she said, I was so hurt I forgot for sixty years to be anything else. I don't want to do that again."
pages.image: A close-up view of a large troll's grey-green hands holding a small white teacup, with a small freckled girl standing in front of him in a dimly lit stone room, the steam from the tea rising between them.

pages.text:
"I know," Rue whispered. "It doesn't have to be all there is."

Hobb nodded. He reached into his waistcoat pocket, where there were too many pockets for one jacket, and pulled out the horn button. He placed it in Rue's hand. It was warm from his touch.

He looked at her for a long moment. Then he turned the button over in his enormous palm, the way a child might turn a shiny coin, and gave it back to her.

"It's yours," he said. "Willa's, and yours. It was never a payment. It was a seat."

Rue sat down on the stone step. Hobb sat down next to her, his large shoulders filling the space. They sat there for a long time, and they said nothing at all. The moss on the wall grew a little, just a little, in the shape of a closed eye, and then it opened, and the light came in.
pages.image: A large grey-green troll and a small girl in a yellow raincoat sitting side-by-side on stone steps in a mossy archway, the troll's large hand resting gently near the girl's hand, with green moss growing on the stone wall behind them.

pages.text:
When Rue climbed up the steps into the sun, the air felt different. It was lighter, and it smelled of rain and wet stone and the faint, sweet scent of the moss garden.

Gran was standing at the top. She was wearing her best hat, the one with the blue ribbon, and she was leaning on the wooden rail, looking out at the river. She wasn't crying, exactly. Her face was very still, and her hands were holding the rail tight.

She looked at Rue. She didn't say anything. She didn't have to.

Then Gran turned, and she began to walk back down the steps. One at a time. Slowly. Her silver bun was slightly askew, and her flour-dusted sleeves were tucked into her apron. She was going down to sit in the seat. It was sixty years late, but it was right on time.

Rue held the lantern up, and she watched her go.
pages.image: A small girl in a yellow raincoat holding a glowing lantern stands at the top of stone steps, looking down at a silver-haired woman in a blue hat walking slowly down the stairs into a dark archway.
